title: Duration and Convexity: How Much a Bond Moves
summary: One number that predicts a bond's price response to rates, a second that corrects it, and the asymmetry that works in the holder's favour.

lesson.body:
[[duration]] answers a single question: **if yields move 1%, roughly how much does this bond's price move?**

Two versions, and the distinction matters more than it looks.

**Macaulay duration** is the weighted average time until the bond's cash flows arrive, weighted by their [[present-value|present values]]. Measured in years. It is a description of *when* you get paid.

**Modified duration** is Macaulay duration divided by one plus the yield per period. It is a sensitivity: a modified duration of 7.57 means a 100bp rise in yield costs roughly 7.57% of price.

The same number therefore has two readings — a time and a sensitivity — and they are connected for a reason. **A bond that pays you later has more of its value further out, and distant cash flows are more sensitive to the [[discount-rate|discount rate]].** Duration measures both facts at once.

What raises duration: **longer maturity, lower coupon, lower yield.** A zero-coupon bond has duration equal to its maturity exactly, because there is only one cash flow — which is the cleanest case and worth using as the anchor.

**Duration is a straight-line approximation of a curved relationship. [[convexity]] is the correction, and it always works in the bondholder's favour.**

The price-yield relationship for a conventional bond curves upward. So a linear estimate based on duration alone:

**Overstates the loss** when yields rise.

**Understates the gain** when yields fall.

Both errors favour the holder, which is why convexity is a desirable property rather than a nuisance.

The size of the effect grows with the size of the yield move. For 25bp, duration alone is fine. For 100bp it is visible. For 300bp, using duration alone will be materially wrong, and in the direction that makes a portfolio look riskier than it is.

Two places convexity matters practically rather than academically:

**Long bonds have much more of it.** A thirty-year bond's convexity is a large part of its total return profile, and it is why long duration is not simply "more of the same risk".

**Negative convexity exists and is unpleasant.** A [[callable-bond|callable bond]] or a mortgage-backed security has an embedded option held by the borrower. When rates fall the bond gets called or the mortgage refinances, so the price stops rising. **You keep the downside curvature and lose the upside — the asymmetry runs the wrong way, and that is what you are paid a higher yield for.**

**In a portfolio, duration is not a bond property — it is the risk dial, and it is nearly the only interest rate decision that matters.**

The reason is that duration is additive in the way you would hope: a portfolio's duration is the weighted average of its holdings' durations. So a manager expressing a view on rates does it by moving portfolio duration, and one number summarises the whole position.

This makes a few things immediately calculable:

**The size of a rate view.** A portfolio at duration 7 against a benchmark at duration 5 gains or loses roughly 2% for every 100bp move, relative to the benchmark. That is the bet, quantified, and it can be compared with the manager's stated conviction.

**The cost of being wrong.** A 200bp surprise against a duration-7 portfolio is roughly 14% of capital. That number belongs in a risk report and often does not appear.

**Liability matching.** A pension fund with obligations of duration 15 and assets of duration 5 is not conservatively positioned — it is short duration against its liabilities, and a fall in rates makes it worse off despite owning safe bonds. **Duration matching is why apparently cautious portfolios can be badly mismatched, and why "we hold only government bonds" is not a statement about risk.**

lesson.plainReading: The percentage price change is roughly minus modified duration times the yield change, plus a half times convexity times the yield change squared. The first term is the straight line; the second is the curve, and it is always positive.

variables.meaning: convexity — the second-order correction, positive for conventional bonds
the change in yield, as a decimal

lesson.body: The 5% ten-year bond from the previous topic, priced at 92.64 to yield 6%. Its Macaulay duration is 8.02 years, modified duration 7.57, and convexity 72.6.
walkthrough: **Actual price change:** 92.64 falls to 85.95, which is **−7.22%**.
So duration alone overstated the loss by 35bp. Now add the convexity term: ½ × 72.6 × 0.01² = **+0.36%**.
**Duration plus convexity: −7.57% + 0.36% = −7.21%, against an actual −7.22%.** The two-term approximation is accurate to a [[basis-point|basis point]].
Now the asymmetry, which is the point. A 100bp **fall** takes the price to 100.00, a gain of **+7.94%** — against a 7.22% loss for the same move up.
**Read that carefully: 72bp of extra gain for an identical-sized move in the favourable direction, for free, from the shape of the relationship.**
And compare maturities at the same 100bp rise: the two-year version loses **1.82%**, the ten-year **7.22%**, the thirty-year **12.82%**.

Sanity check worth reusing: **modified duration times the yield move, in percent, is your first estimate — and it is an overstatement of any loss.** If a risk report shows a loss larger than duration times the move, something other than duration is in the position: convexity running the wrong way, or credit.

lesson.caption: What moves duration, and by how much
rows: Cash flows arrive later, so more value sits in distant, rate-sensitive payments.
Less value returned early, so the weighted average time to payment is later.
Distant cash flows are discounted less, so they carry more weight.
One cash flow, so no averaging — the cleanest case to reason from.
The issuer's option shortens the expected life exactly when rates fall.

lesson.body:
**Using duration for a large move.** For 300bp the linear estimate is materially wrong. Include convexity, or reprice the bond properly.

**Assuming parallel shifts.** Duration assumes the whole curve moves together. Real curves steepen, flatten and twist, so two portfolios with identical duration can behave very differently. Key-rate durations exist for exactly this.

**Duration on a credit bond.** Duration measures sensitivity to *its own* yield. For a high yield bond, spread moves dominate rate moves, so a duration-based estimate can be swamped by something duration does not measure.

**Ignoring negative convexity.** Callable bonds and mortgage securities have curvature the wrong way round. A duration-based risk system treats them as ordinary bonds until rates fall and they stop appreciating.

**Reporting duration without the benchmark's.** A duration of 7 is meaningless alone. Against a benchmark of 5 it is a 2-year overweight, and that difference is the actual position.

**[[private-credit|Private credit]] is usually described as having almost no duration, and the description is half right in a way worth being precise about.**

The claim rests on floating-rate coupons: if the coupon resets with the reference rate, the price barely moves when rates move. That is genuinely true, and it is why [[direct-lending|direct lending]] held up in price terms through a sharp tightening cycle.

But there are two exposures the low duration does not remove.

**[[credit-spread|Credit spread]] duration.** The loan's value still responds to the market's required spread for that risk. Spread duration can be several years even when interest rate duration is near zero, and spreads move most in exactly the conditions where the borrowers are struggling.

**The borrower's rate sensitivity.** A floating coupon means the borrower's interest bill rises with rates. Duration near zero at the instrument level, and a large exposure at the credit level — the same rate rise that protects your price attacks your borrower's coverage.

**So "low duration" in private credit means low sensitivity to the risk-free curve, and it says nothing about sensitivity to credit conditions or to the borrower's ability to pay.** Both of those are rate-driven, which is why the protection is narrower than the phrase suggests.

**Ask for portfolio duration next to the benchmark's.** The difference is the rate position; the level alone is not.

**Ask what a 200bp surprise costs, in percent of capital.** Duration times the move, and the answer often surprises a committee that has only seen duration in years.

**For a liability-driven portfolio, ask for the duration of the liabilities too.** Assets at 5 against liabilities at 15 is a large short position dressed as caution.

**For anything callable or mortgage-related, ask about convexity, not just duration.** Negative convexity means the position stops participating exactly when the rally happens.

**In private credit, ask for spread duration separately from interest rate duration.** "Low duration" usually refers only to the second, and the first is where the mark-to-market risk sits.

items: Modified duration is a sensitivity: 7.57 means a 100bp rise costs about 7.57% of price. Macaulay duration is the same number read as a weighted average time to payment.
Convexity corrects the straight line and always favours the holder: duration predicted −7.57%, the actual move was −7.22%, and duration plus convexity gave −7.21%.
The identical 100bp move produced +7.94% down and −7.22% up. That 72bp asymmetry is convexity, and negative convexity in callables and mortgages reverses it.
In a portfolio, duration is the rate dial and it is additive — so a duration of 7 against a benchmark of 5 is a quantified 2-year bet, and a 200bp surprise is roughly 14% of capital.

questions.stem: A bond has a modified duration of 7.57. Yields rise 100bp. Approximately what percentage does the price fall? Give a positive number.
questions.explanation: The actual fall was 7.22%, so duration alone overstated the loss by 35bp. That direction is systematic: a duration-only estimate always overstates losses and understates gains, because it ignores the curvature.

questions.stem: Modified duration 7.57, convexity 72.6, yields rise 100bp. What is the two-term estimate of the price change, in percent? Give the sign.
questions.inputHint: −D × Δy + ½ × C × Δy², with Δy = 0.01
questions.explanation: Accurate to a basis point against the true −7.22%. The convexity term is small at 100bp and grows with the square of the move: at 300bp it contributes 3.27%, which is the difference between a usable estimate and a badly wrong one.

questions.stem: Which bond has the highest duration?
choices: A 10-year callable bond with a 6% coupon
rationales: The highest coupon returns the most value early, which gives it the lowest duration of the four.
Correct. With one cash flow at maturity, duration equals maturity exactly — ten years. No coupon returns value early to shorten it.
Lower than the zero and higher than the 8% coupon bond, because some value still arrives early.
The call feature shortens the expected life, so it has the lowest and least stable duration here.
questions.explanation: The zero-coupon case is worth using as a mental anchor: duration equals maturity, and every coupon paid before maturity pulls the number down. That single relationship reproduces all three drivers without memorising them.

questions.stem: "Our direct lending fund has near-zero duration, so rate moves do not affect us." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — floating coupons remove sensitivity to the risk-free curve, but spread duration remains and the borrower's interest bill rises with rates, attacking coverage
False — floating-rate loans have the same duration as fixed-rate bonds
True — floating coupons eliminate interest rate exposure
False — because private credit is marked at cost rather than at market
rationales: Correct. Two exposures survive: the value still responds to required spreads, and the borrower now pays more interest. The same rate rise protects the price and pressures the credit.
They do not — a resetting coupon genuinely removes most rate sensitivity from the instrument's price.
It removes sensitivity to the risk-free curve, which is a narrower claim than "rate moves do not affect us".
Marking policy affects what you see, not the underlying exposure — and it is a separate criticism.
questions.explanation: The sharpest version of the point: in a rate rise the fund's price holds up and its borrowers' coverage ratios fall. The risk did not disappear, it moved from mark-to-market to credit — and it shows up later, in defaults rather than in prices.

questions.stem: A pension fund holds only government bonds with duration 5. Its liabilities have duration 15. Is it conservatively positioned?
choices: Yes — government bonds carry no credit risk
No — it is effectively short duration against its liabilities, so falling rates increase the deficit despite holding safe assets
Yes, provided the bonds are held to maturity
It cannot be assessed without knowing the credit ratings
rationales: Credit risk is only one risk. The mismatch against the liabilities is the larger exposure here.
Correct. Falling rates raise the present value of 15-year liabilities far more than 5-year assets, so the funding position deteriorates while every holding is investment grade.
Holding to maturity protects against price loss on the assets and does nothing about the liabilities repricing.
Ratings are irrelevant to the mismatch, which is entirely about duration.
questions.explanation: This is why liability-driven investment exists and why it can look strange from outside: buying long bonds or receiving in swaps reduces risk in this framework even though it increases sensitivity to rates. Risk is measured relative to the obligation, not relative to cash.

questions.stem: Why is negative convexity in a mortgage-backed security unattractive?
choices: It means the security has a longer maturity than stated
When rates fall, borrowers refinance, so the security stops appreciating — the holder keeps the downside curvature and loses the upside
It means the security pays no coupon
Negative convexity implies the issuer has defaulted
rationales: The effect is on the expected life, and it shortens when rates fall rather than lengthening.
Correct. The borrower holds a prepayment option. Rates fall, mortgages refinance, principal comes back to be reinvested at the new lower rates, and the price stops rising.
Coupons are unaffected; the curvature comes from the prepayment option.
Negative convexity is a structural property of the option, not a credit event.
questions.explanation: It is the same asymmetry as any short option position, which is exactly what it is — the holder has sold prepayment optionality to the borrower. The higher yield is the premium received, and whether it is enough depends on how rates actually move.
